title: The one who left (Chagigah 15a)
hookLine: Elisha ben Abuya left the tradition, yet his student Rabbi Meir kept walking and learning with him

cards: A horse on the road, and a man in the saddle, on a day when Shabbat law doesn't allow riding.

Walking behind him, on foot, is one of the great teachers of the Mishnah, listening, asking questions, learning Torah from the rider. The rider was once his teacher, a sage who has since left the tradition.
The walker is Rabbi Meir. And at a certain point on the road, the rider pulls up and tells his student to turn back. Today's word is the name the rabbis gave the rider.

teach.b: Acher. The other one. His name was Elisha ben Abuya, a great sage who, in the Talmud's telling, broke from the tradition he had taught.
The rabbis stopped using his name and called him Acher, the other.

Tractate Chagigah tells what his student did next. Rabbi Meir didn't stop learning from him. On that Shabbat, Acher rode and Meir walked behind, the two of them trading verses and readings as they went.
Then Acher said: Meir, turn back.
I've been counting my horse's steps, and here is the Shabbat limit. Beyond this point you may not walk. Look at that.
The man who has left still guards his student's Shabbat, and still knows the law down to the step. And Meir answers him: you, too, turn back. Come home.
He says he heard a voice from behind the heavenly curtain, repeating the prophet's call, "Return, ye backsliding children", and adding: all except Acher.
So they part at the boundary, one turning back toward the town, one riding on. The Talmud doesn't tidy this up. It doesn't say Meir was wrong to walk with him, and it doesn't say Acher came back.

It shows a student who refused to let his teacher's leaving end the conversation. Readers differ about what Meir was doing on that road: learning, hoping, loving, or all three. The text keeps the picture.

teach.h: STILL TALKING, UP TO THE LINE.
teach.b: Two people on one road, one on a horse and one on foot, still talking, right up to the line.

how: The story of Elisha ben Abuya and Rabbi Meir is studied in Chagigah and often discussed in Jewish teaching about how to treat people who have left the tradition.

o: a name for a sage who ruled against the majority
the other one: the rabbis' name for a sage who left
a title for a student who outgrew his own master

games.q: who's on the road — tap the pairs.

s: the name the rabbis gave Elisha ben Abuya after he left.
Rabbi Meir stopped learning from his teacher after he left
he walked behind him on Shabbat, still learning.
Acher warned Meir where the Shabbat limit was
he had counted his horse's steps, and told his student to turn back.

games.q: you're Rabbi Meir. your teacher has left the tradition, and he's riding a horse on Shabbat. what do you do?
o: refuse to speak to him again.
walk behind him and keep learning.
games.why: Meir walks behind, learning, until Acher himself stops him at the Shabbat limit. then Meir asks him to come back too.

practice: Bring to mind someone who walked away from something you share: a faith, a family tradition, a team, a circle of friends. You don't have to agree with where they went; just notice whether the two of you have stopped talking.
Then picture walking a little way beside them, still talking.

wordCard.voice: Acher. Hebrew for the other one: the name the rabbis gave Elisha ben Abuya after he left, the teacher his student Rabbi Meir kept walking with. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: other, another. the name for Elisha ben Abuya after he left the tradition.

carryVoice: Your line: he kept walking with him. His leaving didn't end the conversation between them. Rest well.
